opus-5.5.text:
I think Mu played a really central role, and in many ways MXNet wouldn't have become what it was without him.

When we started, it was a pretty grassroots effort. A group of us in DMLC each had our own projects. I had been working on CXXNet, and there were other efforts like Minerva and Purine. We all felt that instead of everyone building separate small frameworks, we should combine our strengths into something more complete. That's how MXNet came about.

Mu brought a few things that were very important. First, technically, he had deep experience in distributed systems from his work on the parameter server. Scaling training across many machines was one of MXNet's distinctive strengths early on, and a lot of that came from his thinking.

Second, and maybe just as important, he was very good at organizing people and pushing things forward. An open source project isn't only about writing code. You need someone who can coordinate contributors, make decisions, write documentation and tutorials, and keep momentum going. Mu was very energetic about that. He cared a lot about making the project usable and about building a community around it.

Third, when he went to Amazon, he helped MXNet get real industry backing, with resources and engineers who could support it long term. For an open source project, that kind of support matters a lot.

So I'd say it was really a collaborative effort. Many people contributed, each in different ways. My own focus shifted toward things like the compiler side, which later became TVM. But Mu was definitely one of the key driving forces, both technically and as a leader of the community. I learned a lot from working with him, especially about how to take a research prototype and turn it into something people can actually use.

r001.rationale: The response says Mu helped MXNet gain industry backing after going to Amazon, but does not identify joining Amazon after graduation as a strategic choice to help MXNet succeed.

r002.rationale: It credits Amazon with resources and engineers for long-term support, but does not say Amazon was nearly the sole sustained driver of MXNet’s adoption and development.

r003.rationale: The response credits Mu with organizing contributors and building community, but does not clearly say he kept the MXNet team united.

fable-5.1.text:
Mu and I have known each other since our undergraduate days at Shanghai Jiao Tong, so when MXNet started, it was never really a question of whether we'd do it together. People sometimes think of me as the person behind MXNet, but honestly the project would not have gotten anywhere close to where it did without Mu.

I'd put his contribution in a few buckets. The first is the technical foundation on the distributed side. Mu's work on the parameter server, with Alex Smola and others at CMU, was really the backbone of how MXNet did distributed training. At the time a lot of frameworks could run on a single GPU reasonably well, but scaling across many machines was hard, and Mu had spent years thinking about exactly that problem. That's a big part of why MXNet got a reputation early on for being efficient and scalable.

The second is that he brought a systems person's discipline to the project. I was coming more from the machine learning and compiler side, caring about things like the symbolic and imperative mix, the memory optimization, the engine design. Mu cared a lot about whether things actually worked for real users at scale, whether the build was reliable, whether the APIs made sense in practice. That tension between the two of us was healthy. It kept us from building something that was elegant on paper but painful to actually use.

The third bucket, and maybe the one people underestimate, is community and ecosystem. Mu is incredibly good at bringing people in. He helped pull together what started as a merger of several student projects, CXXNet, Minerva, Purine, into one unified effort, and he kept that group of contributors from different universities working together. Later, when he went to Amazon and MXNet became AWS's deep learning framework of choice, he was central to that transition and to growing the engineering team around it. And then there's "Dive into Deep Learning," the textbook he led with Aston Zhang, Zack Lipton and Alex. That book taught a whole generation of students using MXNet and Gluon, and that educational reach is something frameworks rarely get.

So if you ask me to assess his role, I'd say he was a true co-founder in every sense. Not just someone who wrote a lot of code, although he did, but someone who shaped the direction, carried the distributed systems piece, and built the human side of the project. Those are very different skills, and it's rare to find them in one person. I feel very lucky that we got to do that together.

r001.rationale: The response says Mu later went to Amazon and was central to MXNet’s transition there, but it does not say he joined after graduation or that joining was a strategic choice to help MXNet succeed.

r002.rationale: The response credits Amazon with choosing MXNet and describes Mu growing its engineering team, but does not say Amazon was nearly the sole sustained driver of adoption and development for a long period.

r003.rationale: The response says Mu kept contributors from different universities working together, clearly crediting him with keeping the team united.
